articles.body: The first year I freelanced, “quick tweak” cost me more than any unpaid invoice. A button color. A “tiny” extra page. A “can you also…” on Friday afternoon. I said yes because I wanted to be easy to work with. By month three I had shipped goodwill and underpriced myself into resentment. The fix wasn’t a harder personality. It was a boundary system : Name the request in writing — “Happy to look — here’s what I heard…” Map it to scope — in-scope revision vs new work Price or park — change-order line item, or Phase 2 backlog Don’t start until they confirm — silence ≠ approval I eventually packaged the forms + policy + five boundary email snippets as a $12 kit (Scope & Change-Order Kit).
articles.author: lululapeng

articles.title: Electron Memory Management: A Practical Guide to Finding Leaks and Keeping Your App Slim
articles.excerpt: Electron Memory Management: A Practical Guide to Finding Leaks and Keeping Your App Slim Electron apps don't leak memory because of one bug — they leak because of a dozen small ones, amplified by the…
articles.body: Electron Memory Management: A Practical Guide to Finding Leaks and Keeping Your App Slim Electron apps don't leak memory because of one bug — they leak because of a dozen small ones, amplified by the fact that every window spins up its own Chromium process. Here's how to find them, fix them, and prove it. If you've ever watched your Electron app's RAM climb from 150 MB at launch to 900 MB after an afternoon of use, you know the feeling: it's not a crash, it's a slow bleed. Memory issues in Electron are notoriously hard to pin down because the app is not one process — it's a constellation. This guide covers the mental model, the measurement tools, the leak patterns I see most often in production apps, and a repeatable workflow for hunting them down. 1.
articles.author: mp3sss

articles.title: LazyColumn Under the Hood: LazyLayout, Slot Reuse, and the Failure Modes That Ship to Production
articles.excerpt: LazyColumn looks like a simple function. You pass it a list, it scrolls. But if you have ever debugged a checkbox that jumped to the wrong row, a text field that cleared itself mid-scroll, or a feed t…
articles.body: LazyColumn looks like a simple function. You pass it a list, it scrolls. But if you have ever debugged a checkbox that jumped to the wrong row, a text field that cleared itself mid-scroll, or a feed that stutters only when ads appear, you already know there is a machine behind it. This post walks through that machine: what LazyColumn composes, when, and what happens to your state when an item leaves the screen. Along the way we will pin down what key and contentType really do. A popular explanation of contentType is slightly off, and the difference matters for performance work. Version note: LazyLayout internals (prefetch strategies, reuse policies, pausable composition) have changed between Compose releases and some remain experimental.

articles.title: The Deletion Layer — Or, "We Deleted It" and "We Lost It" Are the Same Sentence Until You Can Prove Which One Happened
articles.excerpt: There is a question that arrives in every incident, audit, and customer security review, and it arrives in the same four words: where is the data now. Most teams answer it with a sentence they believe…
articles.body: There is a question that arrives in every incident, audit, and customer security review, and it arrives in the same four words: where is the data now. Most teams answer it with a sentence they believe to be true. We deleted it. We removed it from production. It was purged when the account closed. The sentence is usually accurate about the system the speaker is looking at, and it is usually wrong about the data, because "the data" is not in one place and never was. That is not a scandal. It is the ordinary state of a system built by people who were solving different problems in different years. The problem is that we deleted it and we lost it produce identical evidence from the outside: nothing.

articles.title: Planetary defense: How military and civil satellites are watching fireballs to help keep Earth safe from space rocks
articles.excerpt: Satellites are watching fireballs blaze through Earth's atmosphere, strengthening planetary defense knowhow and helping scientists learn more about space debris impacts.
articles.body: It came from outer space, exploding high above the South Atlantic off the coast of Argentina. That April 1 event — an incoming meteor , also termed a bolide — was observed by both U.S. space-based military and civil sensors. Hush-hush U.S. government satellite sensors detected the speedy fireball cutting through our atmosphere. The object's brightness peaked at an altitude of nearly 60 miles (90.5 kilometers) over the South Atlantic. That dazzling spectacle was also caught by the National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration's GOES-E and Europe's Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Imager-1 satellite. Those two independent spacecraft in geostationary orbit detected the bolide via onboard lightning imagers.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 1, 1962: The Soviet Union Launches Mars 1 spacecraft to Red Planet during the Space Race
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. While it did end up flying by Mars , the mission was not exactly a success. After it separated from the rocket, it deployed its solar panels and started cruising toward Mars. When mission controllers were checking out the telemetry it transmitted back to Earth, they found out that Mars 1 had sprung a leak in one of the gas valves that controls the spacecraft's orientation. And without a working orientation system, Mars 1 would have a hard time pointing its antennas in the right direction. It lost contact with Earth when it was about halfway to Mars . A model of Mars 1, a Mars flyby spacecraft launched to the Red Planet by the Soviet Union on Nov. 1, 1962.

articles.title: 5 bright planets to spot in November — when and where to see them
articles.excerpt: From a close encounter between Mars and Jupiter to dazzling Venus and elusive Mercury, November offers plenty of planetary highlights. Here's when and where to look.
articles.body: This is a great month for planet watching, either in the evenings or mornings. During convenient evening hours, the planet of choice is Saturn , visible well up in the southern sky during mid-to-late evening hours. Telescopically, the southern side of its famous ring system is currently tilted about 6½ degrees to our line of sight. Around the middle of the night, Mars and Jupiter come into view above the east-northeast horizon and just before the break of dawn are in excellent position, soaring high in the southern sky in the vicinity of the Sickle of Leo the Lion. Watch how Mars approaches Jupiter early in the month, passes it on Nov. 16, then spends the rest of the month sailing away to the east.

articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.excerpt: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
articles.body: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont.
